reader_situation: A US homeowner or renter looking at a high electric bill wants to know which appliance is quietly using the most power, and whether it is worth replacing or changing how they use it.
direct_answer: Nationally, air conditioning (19%), space heating (12%) and water heating (12%) are the three largest shares of home electricity use (EIA, 2020). Per home that has them, an electric water heater averages about 2,700 kWh a year, and pool pumps, EV charging, electric heat and central AC each average roughly 2,300-2,500 kWh. Dehumidifiers (about 1,000 kWh) and second refrigerators (about 500 kWh) are the overlooked ones.
consensus: Heating, cooling and water heating are the biggest electricity users.
Use watts x hours / 1,000 x rate to estimate one appliance.
Phantom loads from chargers are small individually.
A plug-in watt meter or utility usage data shows real consumption.
gaps: The old article's per-appliance ranges (e.g., water heater 3,000-4,500 kWh, AC 1,500-4,000 kWh) had no source. EIA's 2020 RECS gives measured averages per household using each end use: water heating 2,706 kWh, space heating 2,484, AC 2,318, clothes dryers 680, lighting 654, all refrigerators 839, TVs 632.

Climate swings the ranking: in hot-humid regions AC averages 4,173 kWh versus 1,310 in very cold and cold regions; electric space heating averages 2,876 kWh in cold regions; water heating is 3,073 kWh in the marine region.

The items most lists skip are among the largest where present: pool pumps 2,384 kWh, EV charging 2,363 kWh, hot tub heaters 1,479 plus 484 for the pump, dehumidifiers 999 kWh, second refrigerators 494 kWh, separate freezers 570 kWh.
Furnace and AC blower fans (air handlers) add 233 kWh for heating and 457 kWh for cooling on average, which most tables omit.
A heat pump water heater saves a household of four about 3,760 kWh a year according to ENERGY STAR ($550 at its assumed 14.6 cents/kWh).
ENERGY STAR says halving pool pump speed cuts its energy to one-eighth, the reason variable-speed pumps save so much.
Heat pump clothes dryers use around 70% less energy than conventional dryers (ENERGY STAR).
Old refrigerators (over 15 years) can cost about $95 more a year to run; an old fridge uses about 20% more energy than an ENERGY STAR model.

evidence.claim: Largest national shares of home electricity
evidence.detail: The three largest categories and their shares of residential site electricity consumption in 2020: air conditioning 19%, space heating 12%, water heating 12%. Lighting and refrigerators are the next two largest. The average U.S. household consumes about 10,500 kWh of electricity per year.
evidence.source_title: Electricity use in homes - U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA)

evidence.claim: Average kWh per household using each end use, part 1 (all homes)
evidence.detail: RECS 2020 Table CE5.3a, kWh per household using the end use: space heating 2,484 (includes main and secondary heating); air handlers for heating 233; air conditioning 2,318; air handlers for cooling 457; ceiling fans 226; dehumidifiers 999; humidifiers 139; water heating 2,706; clothes washers 69; clothes dryers 680; lighting 654; electric vehicle charging 2,363. On-site solar generation is included in consumption.
evidence.source_title: Table CE5.3a Detailed household site electricity end-use consumption, part 1 - averages, 2020 (EIA RECS)

evidence.detail: Table CE5.3a by climate region (kWh per household using the end use). Very cold and cold: space heating 2,876, AC 1,310, water heating 2,669. Mixed-humid: space heating 2,975, AC 2,293, water heating 2,927. Mixed-dry and hot-dry: space heating 951, AC 2,691, water heating 2,065. Hot-humid: space heating 1,914, AC 4,173, dehumidifiers 1,368, water heating 2,559. Marine: space heating 2,696, AC 902, water heating 3,073.
evidence.source_title: Table CE5.3a Detailed household site electricity end-use consumption, part 1 - averages, 2020 (EIA RECS)

evidence.claim: Average kWh per household using each end use, part 2 (all homes)
evidence.detail: RECS 2020 Table CE5.3b, kWh per household using the end use: all refrigerators 839; most-used refrigerator 617; second refrigerators 494; separate freezers 570; cooking 290; microwaves 107; dishwashers 112; all TVs and related 632; most-used TV 210; pool pumps 2,384; hot tub pumps 484; hot tub heaters 1,479. Hot-humid region: pool pumps 2,864.
evidence.source_title: Table CE5.3b Detailed household site electricity end-use consumption, part 2 - averages, 2020 (EIA RECS)

evidence.detail: ENERGY STAR certified heat pump water heaters can save a household of 4 approximately $550 per year on electric bills compared to a standard electric water heater, and more than $5,610 over the lifetime. Table: 3,760 kWh annual savings, electricity price $0.146/kWh, payback 2.7 years.
evidence.source_title: Heat Pump Water Heaters: Benefits and Savings | ENERGY STAR

evidence.claim: Heat pump water heaters lose efficiency in cold spaces
evidence.detail: Heat pump water heaters generally don't operate as efficiently in colder spaces; in cold conditions they may switch temporarily to standard electric heating, which increases energy use during those months.
evidence.source_title: Heat Pump Water Heaters | ENERGY STAR

evidence.detail: Refrigerators over 15 years old could be costing about $95 more per year to run. On average, an old refrigerator uses about 20% more energy than an ENERGY STAR model. If you need a second fridge year-round, replace the old unit with an ENERGY STAR model and recycle the old one.

Reducing pump speed by one-half allows the pump to use just one-eighth as much energy. Certified in-ground pumps use 20% less energy than standard pumps (about $50 a year); above-ground 11% less (about $20 a year).

evidence.claim: Heat pump dryers and lint filter
evidence.detail: Heat pump dryers use around 70% less energy than conventional clothes dryers. A full-size electric ENERGY STAR dryer saves approximately $210 over its life. Clean the lint filter after every load to improve airflow and efficiency.
An ENERGY STAR dehumidifier uses 20% less energy than a similarly sized conventional unit. Optimum RH is generally 30% to 50%. Close doors and windows to the space while the unit runs.

real_questions: Is my AC or my water heater the bigger cost?
Does the old fridge or freezer in the garage really cost much?
How much does a pool pump or hot tub add to the bill?
Is it worth replacing an electric water heater with a heat pump model?
How do I find out which appliance is actually using the power in my house?

original_asset.spec: Table of RECS 2020 average kWh per household using each end use, converted to yearly cost at the registry's 17 cents/kWh with the arithmetic shown (e.g., 2,706 x 0.17 = $460). A climate table showing AC 4,173 kWh in hot-humid vs 1,310 in cold regions. Worked example: heat pump water heater 3,760 kWh saved x 0.17 = $639 a year, versus ENERGY STAR's $550 at 14.6 cents.

cautions: RECS averages apply to households that use that end use; your own home can be far above or below.
Space-heating average includes homes that only use electricity for secondary heat, so whole-house electric heat is likely higher.
Show the formula with the registry rate so readers can use their own; do not invent appliance wattages or prices.
No retrieved source supported a specific water heater temperature setting or blanket/watt meter prices; omit those numbers.
